narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your denial was driven primarily by three factors that strongly signaled a high risk of bar exam failure. The single most influential factor was your class ranking at the end of your third year of law school. You placed in the bottom decile, far below the average student who was accepted. This low ranking was the strongest reason the model predicted you would struggle with the bar. 

The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 24.5, which is well below the average of 37 among accepted students. This also pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Like your third-year ranking, you again placed in the bottom decile, compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students. This further reinforced the model’s concern.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your upper-middle family income and plan to attend full-time, both of which are actually common among accepted applicants.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Once those numbers improve, reapply. Many students successfully gain admission after addressing these exact gaps.
